blocks.text: Examples of OSCE instructions:

items: “Interpret this CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis.”

blocks.text: “A woman presents with acute lower abdominal pain. Describe the CT findings and give your differential diagnoses.”
“A patient with a known ovarian mass has undergone CT staging. Interpret the scan.”
“A woman presents with fever and abdominal pain following pelvic surgery. Assess the CT and discuss management.”
“What are the indications and limitations of CT in a pregnant woman?”
Start by establishing:
Patient and clinical details: Age, symptoms, pregnancy status, last menstrual period and relevant history.
Imaging modality: CT abdomen and pelvis.
Contrast: Determine whether the study is non-contrast, intravenous contrast-enhanced or includes oral/rectal contrast.
Image plane: Axial, coronal or sagittal reconstruction.
Image quality: Check coverage, movement artefact and whether the relevant structures are visible.
Systematic review: Evaluate the abdominal organs, bowel, urinary tract, reproductive organs, peritoneum, lymph nodes, bones and visible soft tissues.

If the patient is of reproductive age, establish pregnancy status when relevant before non-emergency imaging. In a suspected emergency, do not delay essential diagnostic imaging or life-saving care inappropriately.
The most common CT image plane. Imagine looking up from the patient's feet toward the head. The patient's right side appears on the left side of the image.
A frontal reconstruction that helps assess the kidneys, bowel, pelvic organs and the cranio-caudal extent of masses.
A side-on reconstruction useful for assessing the relationship between the bladder, uterus, vagina and rectum.

content_groups.group_title: CT density: what appears white, grey or black?

blocks.text: CT attenuation is measured in Hounsfield units (HU).

rows: Often relatively hyperattenuating on non-contrast CT, but appearance varies

blocks.text: Exam tip: Do not identify blood solely by its colour on a contrast-enhanced image. Correlate attenuation, distribution, the scan phase and clinical context.

subsections.subsection_title: Systematic CT interpretation: the ABCDE approach

blocks.text: Use this framework when the examiner gives you an unfamiliar CT scan.
First identify the study type, contrast phase and image coverage. Then review:
Liver and gallbladder.
Spleen.
Pancreas.
Adrenal glands.
Kidneys and visible collecting systems.
Look for organ enlargement, focal lesions, inflammation, obstruction, abnormal enhancement or traumatic injury.
Assess the stomach, small bowel, colon and appendix where visible.
Look for:
Dilated bowel loops and a transition point.
Bowel wall thickening.
Inflammatory changes.
Free gas suggesting perforation.
Collections or abscesses.
Appendicitis and other causes of acute abdominal pain.
In a woman presenting with lower abdominal pain, appendicitis, diverticulitis, bowel obstruction and urinary tract pathology can mimic gynaecological disease.
Assess the abdominal aorta, inferior vena cava and visible pelvic vessels.
Look for:
Aneurysm or vascular injury.
Active contrast extravasation.
Major venous thrombosis where adequately assessed.
Vascular compression or displacement by a mass.

content_groups.group_title: D — Densities, peritoneum and lymph nodes

blocks.text: Look for:
Free fluid or haemoperitoneum.
Free intraperitoneal gas.
Peritoneal nodules or thickening.
Omental abnormalities.
Enlarged pelvic or para-aortic lymph nodes.
Ascites and evidence of metastatic disease.
In suspected ovarian malignancy, ascites, peritoneal deposits, omental disease and lymphadenopathy are important staging findings.

content_groups.group_title: E — Everything else, especially the pelvis

blocks.text: Review:
Urinary bladder.
Uterus and cervix.
Adnexa, including the ovaries and fallopian tube regions.
Vagina where visible.
Pelvic floor and surrounding soft tissues.
Pelvic bones and hip joints.
Describe any mass by its size, location, composition, margins, enhancement pattern and relationship to adjacent organs.
Remember that normal ovaries may not always be separately identifiable on CT, and CT has limitations in characterising many uterine and adnexal lesions.
Reproductive-age woman with lower abdominal pain.
Amenorrhoea or a positive pregnancy test.
Vaginal bleeding, dizziness or syncope.
Tachycardia, hypotension or shock if rupture and significant haemorrhage have occurred.
High-attenuation free fluid consistent with blood.
An adnexal mass.
Active contrast extravasation in some cases.
Associated pelvic or abdominal blood collections.

Important limitation: CT is not the routine first-line investigation for suspected ectopic pregnancy. Pregnancy testing, quantitative serum β-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound are the usual initial investigations in a stable patient. CT may identify haemoperitoneum when imaging is performed for another reason, or be used in selected circumstances after specialist assessment.

If rupture or haemodynamic instability is suspected, initiate emergency resuscitation and urgent gynaecological assessment. Do not delay operative management in an unstable patient while awaiting further imaging.
Ovarian torsion is twisting of the ovary and sometimes the fallopian tube around its supporting structures, potentially compromising venous and then arterial blood flow.
CT findings may include:
An enlarged, oedematous ovary.
Peripheral displacement of follicles, when discernible.
Twisting of the vascular pedicle or a whirlpool appearance.
Adnexal mass or cyst.
Periovarian fat stranding.
Pelvic free fluid.
Reduced or abnormal ovarian enhancement.
Clinical presentation: Sudden unilateral pelvic pain, often with nausea and vomiting. Symptoms may be intermittent.

Management: Urgent gynaecological review. Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler is generally the first-line imaging study, but preserved Doppler flow does not exclude torsion. When clinical suspicion is high, urgent surgical assessment is required; imaging must not create an unsafe delay.
Complex adnexal masses, sometimes bilateral.
Solid and cystic components.
Ascites.
Peritoneal nodules.
Omental caking.
Pelvic or para-aortic lymphadenopathy.
Possible liver surface deposits or other distant metastases.
Clinical significance: CT is useful for assessing the extent of disease, identifying possible metastases and planning treatment.
Pelvic ultrasound.
CA-125 and other tumour markers as indicated by age, imaging and clinical presentation.
Histological diagnosis when appropriate.
CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging where indicated.
Specialist gynaecological oncology assessment.
Management: Refer to the appropriate specialist team. Treatment may involve surgery and systemic anticancer therapy, depending on the histology, stage, resectability and patient's circumstances.
OSCE caution: CA-125 is not diagnostic of ovarian cancer by itself. It may be elevated in benign conditions, including endometriosis and pelvic inflammatory disease.
Fibroids (leiomyomas) are benign smooth-muscle tumours of the uterus.
Enlarged, lobulated uterus.
Well-defined uterine masses.
Heterogeneous attenuation from degeneration.
Coarse or peripheral calcification in some fibroids.
Displacement or compression of the bladder or bowel.
Limitations: Ultrasound is usually preferred for initial assessment. MRI is more useful when detailed mapping or characterisation is required.
Management: Depends on symptoms, size, location, anaemia, fertility goals and pregnancy status. Options include observation, medical treatment and selected procedures or surgery.

content_groups.group_title: E. Pelvic inflammatory disease and tubo-ovarian abscess

blocks.text: Thickened or enhancing fallopian tubes.
Complex adnexal collection.
Thick-walled rim-enhancing abscess.
Surrounding fat stranding.
Pelvic free fluid.
In severe cases, inflammatory changes extending into adjacent structures.
Clinical features: Pelvic pain, fever, abnormal vaginal discharge, cervical motion tenderness and raised inflammatory markers may be present.
Investigations: Pregnancy test, full blood count, inflammatory markers, STI testing where appropriate, and pelvic ultrasound.

Management: Prompt antibiotics covering likely pathogens, assessment of severity and hospital admission when indicated. Drainage or surgery may be needed for a large or persistent abscess, suspected rupture, diagnostic uncertainty or failure to improve with antibiotics.

content_groups.group_title: F. Postoperative pelvic collection or abscess

blocks.text: This may occur following caesarean section, hysterectomy or other pelvic surgery.
A fluid collection, sometimes with peripheral enhancement.
Surrounding inflammatory change.
Gas within a collection in some cases.
Possible associated bowel, urinary tract or wound complications.
Differential diagnoses: Abscess, haematoma, seroma, urinoma or bowel leak, depending on the procedure and scan findings.

Management: Assess for sepsis, obtain appropriate laboratory investigations and cultures when indicated, begin antibiotics when infection is suspected, and seek surgical review. Image-guided drainage or reoperation may be required depending on the source and severity.

subsections.subsection_title: CT abdomen and pelvis in pregnancy

blocks.text: This is an important viva topic because you must balance diagnostic accuracy against radiation exposure.
Significant maternal trauma.
Suspected appendicitis when ultrasound and MRI are unavailable, inconclusive or unsuitable for the clinical situation.
Suspected bowel perforation or obstruction.
Serious vascular pathology.
Other potentially life-threatening conditions that cannot be adequately assessed with safer or more appropriate alternatives.

content_groups.group_title: Which imaging modality should you choose?

rows: Characterisation of an indeterminate pelvic mass
Ultrasound, then MRI when available and appropriate; CT may be necessary if uncertainty persists
Trauma-directed imaging, including CT when indicated
Ultrasound and contrast-enhanced CT for staging; MRI may help characterise selected lesions

blocks.text: CT uses ionising radiation. Fetal exposure depends on the scan protocol, the anatomical region and the gestational stage.
A medically necessary CT should not be withheld when delaying diagnosis could harm the mother or fetus.
Use appropriate dose optimisation.
Iodinated intravenous contrast may be used when it materially improves diagnosis. Its use in pregnancy should be justified by the clinical indication and local policy.
Discuss individual concerns with radiology and obstetric teams when appropriate.
OSCE model answer:

“I would first establish the clinical indication and pregnancy status. Ultrasound or MRI may be preferable for many pelvic conditions in pregnancy, but if CT is necessary to diagnose a serious maternal condition, I would not delay essential imaging. I would discuss the indication with radiology, optimise radiation exposure and balance the risks of imaging against the risks of a missed or delayed diagnosis.”

subsections.subsection_title: How to distinguish important CT findings

rows: Abscess, infected collection or selected postoperative complications
Complex adnexal mass with ascites and peritoneal nodules
Ovarian malignancy is an important consideration
Enlarged oedematous ovary with twisted pedicle
Enlarged irregular uterus with well-defined masses
Dilated bowel with a transition point
Possible bowel perforation or postoperative free gas, depending on context
Urinary tract obstruction, which may be caused by a stone, mass or pregnancy-related compression
Malignancy, infection or other causes of lymphadenopathy

blocks.text: These findings must be interpreted in the context of the patient's history, the CT technique and the complete scan.

subsections.subsection_title: How to report a CT in the OSCE

blocks.text: Use this sequence:
Patient and indication → Modality and contrast → Findings → Impression → Recommendations.

content_groups.group_title: Example 1: Normal CT abdomen and pelvis

blocks.text: “This is a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis. The visualised abdominal organs show no significant acute abnormality. There is no bowel obstruction or free intraperitoneal gas. No significant free fluid is identified. The uterus and adnexal regions show no obvious acute abnormality on this examination. There is no obvious pelvic lymphadenopathy. Overall, there is no definite acute CT abnormality identified. Clinical correlation and further investigation would be guided by the presenting symptoms.”
Only use this report if those findings are actually demonstrated on the supplied images.

“The CT demonstrates a complex, thick-walled adnexal collection with surrounding inflammatory changes and adjacent pelvic fluid. In the appropriate clinical context, this is concerning for a tubo-ovarian abscess. Differential diagnoses include other infected pelvic collections and complicated adnexal pathology. I would recommend urgent gynaecological assessment, inflammatory markers, appropriate microbiological investigations and prompt treatment.”

“The CT demonstrates a complex adnexal mass with ascites, peritoneal nodularity and omental abnormalities. These findings are concerning for ovarian malignancy with possible peritoneal dissemination. I would recommend specialist gynaecological oncology review, appropriate tumour-marker assessment, histological diagnosis when indicated and staging investigations to guide treatment.”

Failing to identify whether intravenous contrast was used.
Forgetting that the patient's right side is displayed on the left of an axial image.
Focusing on the pelvis while overlooking bowel obstruction, perforation or vascular emergencies.
Diagnosing ectopic pregnancy from CT alone without considering pregnancy testing and ultrasound.
Assuming normal Doppler flow excludes ovarian torsion.
Calling every pelvic collection an abscess without considering a haematoma or other collection.
Diagnosing ovarian cancer from CA-125 or a CT appearance alone without appropriate further assessment.
Assuming CT is absolutely prohibited during pregnancy.
Delaying urgent treatment of haemorrhage, torsion, sepsis or suspected perforation while awaiting additional tests.
